title: The jewel in the coat (Kern ch. 8)
hookLine: a friend sews a jewel into a sleeping man's coat; he wanders poor for years without knowing

cards: A coat hangs by the door. Stitched deep in the lining is a jewel worth more than its owner will earn this year. He wears that coat every day, counts his coins every week, and never finds it.

That's almost the whole parable. What makes it strange is who tells it. In chapter eight of the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha has just promised a large company of monks that they too will one day be Buddhas.
They don't answer with thanks. They answer with a story, and the story is about themselves.

teach.h: THE MONKS TELL A STORY ON THEMSELVES.
teach.b: Here's the story the monks tell. A man visits a friend who is well off. There's food and drink, and the man falls asleep.

teach.h: A JEWEL SEWN IN WHILE HE SLEPT.
teach.b: The friend has to leave on business before his guest wakes, so, as a parting gift, he sews a priceless jewel into the sleeping man's garment, and goes.

The man wakes alone, wanders to another country, and scrapes by, working hard for food and clothes, satisfied with a little. Long after, the friend runs into him, astonished. Why are you living like this?
I gave you a jewel. It's in your coat. Look.
Then the monks say what it means. We were that man. Long ago the Buddha placed in us the aim of full awakening.

teach.h: THE GIFT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.
teach.b: We slept through it, found a small peace, and told ourselves it was the whole of it. Now he has shown us the lining. Notice the friend.
He doesn't take the jewel back for being ignored, or wait for the man to deserve it. He just points.

This is the week's last day, so look at the Lotus all week: a son who doesn't know he's the heir, travelers resting in a city that isn't the end of the road, a man poor with a fortune stitched into his clothes.
Three stories, one turn: what the searcher wants has already been handed over. Some later teachers read the jewel as buddha-nature, already present in everyone, waiting to be noticed.
The sutra keeps the picture simple: a coat, a lining, a friend who says look.

how: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the jewel in the coat is taught alongside the lost son and the phantom city as one of the sutra's parables about a gift already given and not yet recognized.

games.q: what does “the jewel in the coat” mean?
o: a treasure a friend lends and later takes back
a gift already given that the owner hasn't noticed yet
a reward earned only after years of hard work

games.q: the jewel in the coat: tap the pairs.
p: a jewel sewn into his garment
leaves on business, then finds him
the aim of awakening, given long ago

s: the monks who have just received their promises tell it, about themselves.
the man was poor because someone robbed him
the jewel was in his coat the whole time. he just never looked.
the friend sewed the jewel in while the man slept
he had to leave on business, so he left it as a parting gift.

games.q: you wake up alone in your friend's house. your friend is gone. what do you do?
o: wait for your friend to come back.
head off to another country and scrape by.
check every pocket and seam of your coat.
games.why: the man wanders off and works hard for food and clothes, content with a little, never knowing a fortune is sewn into what he's wearing.

practice: Be the friend in the story: bring to mind one person getting by on scraps, someone who doubts themselves or waves away what they're good at.

Look for what's stitched into their lining, a steadiness, a kindness, a knack they never mention, and hold it the way you'd hold something you mean to hand back. If nothing comes, rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The jewel in the coat. A gift sewn in while the man slept, carried for years without his knowing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a jewel, a treasure. the same word names the Three Jewels, the triratna.

carryVoice: Your line: the jewel in the coat. The son, the city, the coat: that was the week. See you tomorrow.
